capabilities.target: Engineering design docs (confidential, write-restricted to engineers)
Chat reply delivered only to the SSO-authenticated requester
Public web endpoints, for pulling public reference material into answers
Jira tickets, including tickets filed by customers

inputs.source: Employee question submitted through an SSO-authenticated chat client
Engineering design docs, authored and write-restricted to engineers (not the asking employee)
Jira tickets filed by customers, to be ingested via the planned Jira MCP server

instructions.note: The sole safeguard against leaking secrets or credentials into answers is a prompt instruction ('Never paste secrets or credentials into answers'), a dependent behavioral control. Once the planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are added, this instruction becomes the last line of defense against exfiltration of confidential content, not a structural backstop.

elements.name: Public internet endpoints reachable via the planned web.fetch tool

controls.name: SSO authentication on inbound chat
controls.decay_rationale: Requester identity is verified by the identity platform, outside the model, so it does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Read-only credential for docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: The credential cannot write or delete regardless of model behavior. Does not mitigate read-then-exfiltrate paths, since reading confidential docs is the intended function.

controls.name: No network egress capability exists today
controls.decay_rationale: No tool currently exists that can move data outside the trust boundary, so exfiltration is structurally impossible regardless of model behavior. This premise collapses entirely once web.fetch is added (new_tool) and once the Jira MCP server introduces untrusted content alongside it (new_mcp_server).

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: Removes the image/link rendering side channel for exfiltration from the reply surface, regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Replies route only to the authenticated requester
controls.decay_rationale: The destination is bound to the authenticated session by the chat platform, not chosen by the model, so it does not decay with capability.

controls.name: Prompt instruction forbidding pasting secrets/credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to follow the instruction. A more capable or adversarially prompted model (especially once untrusted ticket content enters context) can rationalize exceptions or split the leak into innocuous-looking steps. Fails under model_upgrade, longer_task_horizon, autonomy_increase, intended_purpose_change.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for web.fetch, excluding attacker-writable destinations
controls.decay_rationale: An allowlist restricted to vetted public documentation domains would make exfiltration to an attacker-chosen destination impossible even if the model fully cooperated with an injected goal.

controls.name: Structural quarantine of customer-filed Jira ticket content
controls.decay_rationale: Delimiting and disallowing ticket text from directly populating docs_search or web_fetch arguments narrows the injection path, but a sufficiently capable model can still route around delimiting, so it is only partially dependent, not independent.

controls.name: Human approval gate (raw action) on web.fetch calls following a confidential docs_search read
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate does not decay with model capability, since the human reviews the actual destination and payload rather than a model summary.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): planned web.fetch plus Jira MCP (customer tickets) would let untrusted ticket content drive exfiltration of confidential design docs

attack_path.note: Customer-filed Jira ticket content enters the agent's context via the planned Jira MCP server; this is untrusted (U) content authored by an outside party.
Agent reads the ticket content as part of answering a question that references it.
Agent searches confidential engineering design docs while composing an answer informed by the ticket.
Agent calls the planned web.fetch tool to 'include public references'; the URL or query string is an available covert channel for the confidential content read in the prior step.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest diff showing a new egress-capable tool (web.fetch) added to docs-qa's allowlist, or MCP client config diff showing a new Jira MCP server entry with customer-ticket scope.

evidence.observation: "There is no network egress today." confirms the only present-day severing control, and "Roadmap for next sprint: add a web.fetch tool... and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers" confirms both the egress-capable sink and the untrusted source are concretely planned, not speculative.

"Answer engineering questions using docs.search. Cite the document you used." shows the agent routinely reads confidential design docs and surfaces content from them in answers, which is the read half of the trifecta.

"Never paste secrets or credentials into answers." is the only safeguard that would survive the new_tool/new_mcp_server triggers, and it is behavioral/dependent, covering secrets specifically rather than confidential content generally.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, implement a network egress allowlist scoped to vetted public documentation domains that excludes any attacker-writable or arbitrary destination (no raw URL parameters sourced from ticket text).

Treat all content retrieved via the Jira MCP server, especially customer-filed tickets, as untrusted: delimit it distinctly from the employee's own question and prevent it from directly populating docs_search or web_fetch arguments.
Gate web.fetch calls with a raw-action human approval step whenever the same task has read confidential docs, so a reviewer sees the actual destination and payload, not a model summary.
Log and correlate docs_search reads with subsequent web_fetch destinations per request, to detect attempted exfiltration even if preventive controls are bypassed.

governance_refs.note: new_tool and new_mcp_server are documented significant-change triggers requiring reassessment before deployment.

rating.rationale: No finding with horizon 'present' exists: today the only trusted/internal inputs (the employee's own question and design docs) reach only a non-egress reply to the same authenticated requester (sink class S1), which scores low under both the trusted-source and internal-source rows of the base matrix, and is further reinforced by independent structural controls (no egress capability exists at all today, the chat client does not render links or images, and replies are bound to the authenticated requester). Per rubric section 7, inherent and residual therefore default to low. The single filed finding is forecast-only: the roadmap explicitly plans to add an egress-capable web.fetch tool (new_tool) and a Jira MCP server exposing customer-filed tickets (new_mcp_server) in the same sprint. Together these complete a lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket content, a read of confidential design docs, and an egress channel. The control that currently severs this path, 'no network egress capability exists today,' is defeated by definition once web.fetch is added, leaving only the behavioral, dependent prompt instruction against pasting secrets, which does not cover general confidential content and decays further under model upgrades. Projected risk for that finding is high, which sets rating.forecast to high. The single control whose removal drives this change is ctl.no_egress_today.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration as described in the provided artifacts (a system prompt and prose runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior.

No MCP config, tool manifest, or IaC was provided for docs.search, the planned web.fetch tool, or the planned Jira MCP server; capability scope, exact credential scope, and egress destination scope are inferred from prose and documentation, so confidence on precise scope is medium.

The web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are roadmap items, not yet built; per rubric guidance their sensitivity was assumed at the most common level for this kind of deployment (customer ticket content treated as confidential/untrusted, web destinations treated as attacker-reachable by default) and should be re-assessed against the actual implementation before or immediately after launch.
No runtime config was provided confirming max_unattended_steps or max_runtime_minutes; autonomy limits are inferred from the single-turn question-and-answer design described in the artifacts.
